# Notes on 2 Samuel 19:1–22

**What I covered:** Enduring Word (Guzik), Ellicott, Gill, Pulpit Commentary, Expositor's Bible, Matthew Henry, Clarke, Coffman, Precept Austin, and the Bible Hub study notes and commentary pages for individual verses.

**What I didn't find:** I didn't reach any NET Bible notes, anything from Bible Odyssey, or any Catholic or Orthodox commentary (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org). I also found nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers on this passage. None of those appear below.

**On differences between traditions:** I found no disagreement that clearly follows denominational lines. The real disagreements are between individual commentators. I've marked them ⚖️ and labelled a commentator's tradition only where a source states it.

---

**v. 1**
- Gill: Joab probably heard the report as he returned to Mahanaim, or on the way, before he saw the king. David was mourning when he should have been celebrating the victory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Bible Hub note: in the Hebrew Bible this verse is the start of chapter 19. The King James Version (KJV) follows the Greek and Latin chapter division. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/19-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: David's loyal supporters won that day for the glory of God and the good of Israel. Then they felt bad about the victory because David was overcome with excessive weeping and mourning for Absalom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/
- Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew word translated "victory" is literally "salvation." The people did not understand the poignant emotions caused by the activity of David's conscience, and were pained at this seeming ingratitude. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-19.html
- Expositor's Bible: notes how little is said about the twenty thousand who died in the battle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 3**
- Gill: the soldiers didn't march in triumph. They slipped in one by one, as if they had been beaten or had run away, afraid they had displeased the king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Guzik: David's excessive sorrow made his supporters feel ashamed of winning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/

**v. 4**
- Clarke: This was the custom of mourners. O my son Absalom — Calmet has properly remarked that the frequent repetition of the name of the defunct, is common in the language of lamentation. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/2-samuel-19.html
- Gill: the mourning probably went on for some time, perhaps days, since the army had already come back. A short outburst on first hearing the news would have been more excusable, but this went too far. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Matthew Henry imagines David's thought: "He is dead; and, dying in sin, I fear he is lost for ever." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_019.cfm
- Guzik: on the parallel cry in 18:33, he says the soil for Absalom's rebellion came partly from David's indulgent parenting, and that David saw his sins, his weaknesses, and his rebellion exaggerated in Absalom. https://enduringword.com/anguish-father/
- Bible Hub study notes: this verse's notes say the lament can be seen as a type of Christ, as it echoes the sorrow of God the Father over the rebellion and sin of humanity. https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/19-4.htm
- Expositor's Bible: grief should not be pushed on others, especially by someone in public life. It points to Christ, who kept his own sorrow largely private. David was on the very eve of losing the affections of those who had risked everything for him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: This is a continuation of 2Samuel 19:1, the intervening verses being parenthetical. Joab, with Absalom's blood on his hands, rebukes the father in harsh, insolent terms. Yet he still gives wise and loyal advice. Ellicott doubts David yet knew Joab's part in Absalom's death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Ellicott on "the lives of thy sons": had Absalom won, he would probably have killed his father and every possible rival for the throne, as Eastern rulers often did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 6**
- Gill: "you love your enemies" was not strictly true but was greatly exaggerated. David would have liked Absalom to live, but not at the cost of his army's lives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Guzik: Joab wanted David not only to see that he was foolish in his excessive grief, but he was also selfish. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/

**v. 7** ⚖️ *What did Joab's oath mean?*
- Gill: Joab was hinting that he would use his influence to lead the army away and set up another king. Gill also thinks Joab spoke above his place as a subject. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Ellicott disagrees. Joab does not seem to have conceived, far less to have expressed any such design. The oath simply stresses how dangerous David's course was, put strongly enough to shake him out of his selfish grief. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: David let his understanding of what was right override what he felt. Seeing him sitting in the gate told the people their sacrifice was valued. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/
- Ellicott: "Israel" here, as throughout this story, means Absalom's followers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Gill agrees that "Israel" refers to Absalom's followers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: once the rebellion collapsed, the people's infatuation passed and they remembered what they owed David. But the movement to restore him had no organisation or leader. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Gill: every tribe except Judah blamed one another. David's past rescues made their rebellion worse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Guzik applies it to believers: we often only decide to bring back King Jesus when our false kings fail. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: Absalom's anointing is mentioned nowhere else, and the high priests would not have performed it. A prophet may have done it, or the phrase may just mean "appointed." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Gill: either it really happened or Absalom was simply proclaimed king. His death shows the thing was not of God and freed them from their oath to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: Judah was slow because it had been the cradle of the rebellion. Jerusalem probably still had a garrison of Absalom's soldiers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Gill: Judah was afraid of David's resentment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Guzik: David would not force his reign on Israel. He would only come back if the tribes who rejected him for Absalom agreed to bring back the king. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: what would sway Judah was that the king acknowledged their blood tie to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Gill: being his own flesh, they could expect gentle treatment, since he was so ready to forgive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 13** ⚖️ *Was offering Amasa the command wise?*
- Ellicott: David adopted a bold, but a rash and unjust policy. Amasa should have been punished, not rewarded for his treason. David wanted to be rid of Joab now that Joab had killed Absalom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Gill gives the same motive: Joab's murder of Abner, his killing of Absalom against orders, and his insolence. Amasa's appointment also pardoned and won over Absalom's general. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Joab could only have been removed by killing him, which he didn't deserve. Joab was also the better general. David was, in fact, blinded by love for the son whom for so many years he had treated with coldness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 14**
- Gill: Jewish commentators generally say the "he" who swayed Judah was Amasa. Gill thinks it was David, winning hearts through gentle messages when he could have returned by force. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Guzik: their hearts could not be forced; they had to be swayed. He applies this to God's kingship, which does not coerce. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/

**v. 15**
- Pulpit Commentary: Gilgal, on the west bank near Jericho and the fords, was a convenient place for Judah's elders to wait. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-19.html
- Guzik: David would not return until he was welcomed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/

**v. 16** ⚖️ *Was Shimei sincere?* (continues through v. 22)
- Ellicott: Shimei had influence, and his support was valuable. But he was only a time-server, and that he was thoroughly disloyal in his heart. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Gill: Shimei hurried to ask pardon so he would not fall victim to David's revenge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Matthew Henry: had David lost, Shimei would have kept trampling on him. He applies it to those who will want to make peace with the Son of David too late. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_019.cfm

**v. 17**
- Gill: the thousand Benjamites may have been a military unit Shimei commanded, his tenants, or people brought along to plead for him. Ziba came early because he knew Mephibosheth would expose his lie. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- Ellicott: "before the king" means "to meet the king." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 18**
- Gill reads the KJV's "ferry boat" for carrying the royal family. He mentions the views that it was a pontoon or men carrying people across. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/19.htm
- A commentator on Bible Hub's verse page argues from the Hebrew that Shimei bowed when David was about to cross, not after. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/19-19.htm

**v. 19**
- Gill: non-imputation of sin is in effect the pardon of it. Shimei asks David to forget as well as forgive. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/19-19.htm
- Geneva Study Bible: in his adversity he was his most cruel enemy, and now in his prosperity, seeks by flattery to creep into favour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/19-19.htm
- Guzik reads Shimei favourably: his repentance was humble, honoured the king, and was honest. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: Shimei was a Benjamite, not strictly of Joseph. "Joseph" stands for all the tribes outside Judah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Guzik: Real repentance will show itself not only in words and ideas but also in action. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/
- Expositor's Bible is harsh: Shimei's bowing came from a base nature that can insult the fallen, but lick the dust off the feet of men in power. He moved only after David's policy of mercy was known. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/2_samuel/19.htm

**v. 21**
- Precept Austin: In theory Abishai may have been correct. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-19-commentary
- Coffman: killing Shimei could have set off a bloody battle, especially if his thousand men were soldiers. Abishai shows how satanic temptations can reach us through those close to us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/19-22.html

**v. 22**
- Ellicott: The word in the original here is Satan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: literally "that ye be to me for a Satan." Ewald translates it "tempter," but it probably means "one who would do me harm." Joab need not have shared Abishai's rashness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-samuel-19.html
- Gill links the word to Peter in Matthew 16:22. Executing the first man to ask pardon would have made all the rebels expect the same and rebel again. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/19-22.htm
- Matthew Henry: Those who advise us to what is wrong are really Satans, adversaries to us. Acts of severity are seldom acts of policy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/19-22.html
- Henry also says: Those that are forgiven must forgive. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_019.cfm
- Guzik: David could readily forgive a man who deserved to die because he was secure, knowing that God gave him the throne. Insecurity is a great motivator for revenge and holding on to bitterness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-19/
- ⚖️ A sharper verdict: one commentator on Bible Hub's verse page says that since David later told Solomon to punish Shimei (1 Kings 2:8–9), this mercy was only a sign of David's weakness, which was not worthy of imitation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/19-22.htm
- Ellicott, looking ahead to v. 23, sees it politically: David made a rash oath and kept it to the letter, but no further, toward a traitor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/19.htm
- Translations: the Catholic Douay-Rheims keeps the word "satan": why are you a satan this day to me? The Greek Septuagint has ye as it were lie in wait against me this day. https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/19-22.htm

---

### Summary of the main disagreements
1. **v. 7, Joab's oath:** Gill reads it as a veiled threat to lead the army away; Ellicott reads it as a warning only.
2. **v. 13, Amasa:** Ellicott calls the appointment rash and unjust; the Pulpit Commentary says David was "blinded by love."
3. **vv. 16–22, Shimei:**
   - **Sincere:** Guzik (Enduring Word, which is in your Pentecostal/charismatic group).
   - **A time-server or flatterer:** Ellicott, whose editor was Anglican; Ellicott's Bible Hub index calls him LATE LORD BISHOP OF GLOUCESTER (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/index.html). The Geneva Study Bible and Expositor's Bible say the same.
   - **David's mercy was weakness:** the unnamed Bible Hub commentator on v. 22.
   - **Gill**, whom StudyLight labels John Gill · Baptist · Calvinism (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/19-40.html), takes a middle line: Shimei acted out of self-preservation, but David's pardon was wise.

These are differences between individual writers. None of the pages I read present them as positions of a whole tradition.
